**Duel with Aaron Burr**
On July 11, 1804, sitting Vice President Aaron Burr fatally shot Hamilton in a duel at Weehawken, New Jersey. They fought there because New York had outlawed dueling, near the spot where Hamilton's son Philip had been killed in a duel in 1801. Hamilton's own shot struck a tree above Burr, and seconds such as Burr's William P. Van Ness later gave conflicting accounts of what happened.

**First Secretary of the Treasury**
Hamilton served as the first US Treasury Secretary under George Washington (1789–1795). In that role he also founded the US Mint and the Revenue Cutter Service, the forerunner of the Coast Guard. He appears on the ten-dollar bill and is the subject of Lin-Manuel Miranda's musical Hamilton.

**The Federalist Papers and "Publius"**
A series of 85 essays (1787–1788) urging New York to ratify the Constitution, written under the shared pseudonym "Publius" by Hamilton, James Madison, and John Jay. Hamilton wrote 51 of them, the most of the three authors.

**Report on Public Credit and assumption of state debts**
Hamilton's 1790 First Report on Public Credit proposed that the federal government take on ("assume") the states' Revolutionary War debts and repay federal securities at full face value ("funding at par"), backed by a sinking fund. He later issued further reports on public credit.

**First Bank of the United States**
A national bank created in 1791 at Hamilton's urging. Jefferson argued it was unconstitutional, while Hamilton defended it on the basis of the Constitution's implied powers, and it was a founding issue in the split between Federalists and Democratic-Republicans.

**Report on Manufactures**
Hamilton's 1791 report urging the government to encourage American industry through protective tariffs and "pecuniary bounties" (subsidies). It became a foundation of the "American School" of economics. He also inspired the Society for Establishing Useful Manufactures, which developed Paterson, New Jersey, as an industrial center.

**Maria Reynolds affair**
Hamilton had an affair with Maria Reynolds, whose husband James Reynolds then blackmailed him. When the payments surfaced and an investigation involving James Monroe seemed to suggest financial corruption, Hamilton published a pamphlet in 1797 admitting the affair. The scandal damaged his reputation and nearly led to a duel with Monroe.

**Federalist No. 78 ("neither FORCE nor WILL")**
Hamilton's essay "The Judiciary Department," which calls the courts the "least dangerous," or weakest, of the three branches, citing Montesquieu. He argued the judiciary has "neither FORCE nor WILL, but merely judgment," and the essay also defends judicial review.

**Federalist No. 70 ("Energy in the Executive")**
Hamilton's essay arguing for a single executive rather than a council, because a unitary executive provides "decision, activity, secrecy, and dispatch." It cites the instability caused by ancient Rome's two consuls.

**Whiskey tax and the Whiskey Rebellion**
To raise revenue to pay the assumed debts, Hamilton proposed an excise tax on whiskey. Western Pennsylvania farmers revolted against it in the 1794 Whiskey Rebellion, which Washington and Hamilton suppressed with militia.

**Compromise of 1790**
At a dinner with Thomas Jefferson and James Madison, Hamilton won Southern support for assuming state debts in exchange for placing the national capital on the Potomac River, the future Washington, D.C.

**Election of 1800 and Jefferson as the "lesser evil"**
When Jefferson and Burr tied in the Electoral College, Hamilton urged Federalists in the House to support Jefferson, whom he considered less dangerous than Burr. That year he also damaged his own party by publishing a letter attacking John Adams. His continuing opposition to Burr, including in the 1804 New York governor's race that Burr lost to Morgan Lewis, led to the duel.

**Early life and pre-war writings**
Hamilton was born in the British West Indies on Nevis and grew up on St. Croix, where his vivid letter describing a hurricane in Christiansted led locals to pay for his education in New York. As a student at King's College, he defended the Patriot cause against the Loyalist bishop Samuel Seabury in "A Full Vindication" and "The Farmer Refuted," and he once helped the Loyalist college president Myles Cooper escape an angry mob.

**Revolutionary War service and Yorktown**
Hamilton commanded a New York artillery company and then served for years as aide-de-camp to George Washington. At the 1781 Siege of Yorktown he led the night assault that captured Redoubt No. 10.

**Annapolis Convention and the Constitutional Convention**
At the 1786 Annapolis Convention, which he attended for New York with Egbert Benson, Hamilton drafted the report calling for a convention to revise the Articles of Confederation. When his fellow New York delegates Robert Yates and John Lansing left the 1787 Constitutional Convention, he became the only New Yorker to sign the Constitution.

**Pacificus and Camillus essays**
Hamilton wrote as "Pacificus" in 1793 to defend Washington's Neutrality Proclamation in a pamphlet debate with Madison ("Helvidius"). He wrote as "Camillus" to defend the unpopular Jay Treaty with Britain, and he also helped draft Washington's Farewell Address.
